page.layout: One page of running text in one column; in the left margin one marginal note "Cap.3." beside the paragraph. Running head at the top above the text; no page number beyond the running head. Last line of the text is a short full line ending "poris"; no catchword, no signature.

main_text.p: cere ac conferuari. Quare toto errant cœ-lo, qui similitudinem fœtus ad quemlibet masculum, aut fœmellam, imaginationi fœminæ concipientis referunt. Accidit enim hæc formæ similitudo non conceptionis tempore, sed conformationis singularum corporis partium. Etenim conceptio nihil est aliud, quàm utriusque feminis miscella & retentio in utero, quemadmodum explicat Galenus libro, de Formatione fœtus in utero. Adde quòd conceptus non actu est animatus, sed duntaxat potentia, sicuti docet Philosophus libro, de Generatione animalium secundo. Animam vegetalem (inquit) in feminibus, conceptibus, scilicet nondum separatis, haberi potentia statuendum est, non actu, priusquam eo modo, quo conceptus, qui iam separatur, cibum trahant, & officio eius animæ fungantur. Principio enim hæc omnia uitam stirpis uiuere uidentur. Quum igitur conceptus non sit actu animatus, ipsum nô posse quic quam effingere consequens est. Est enim anima omnium actionum causa primaria: calor autem & spiritus, atque membra duntaxat instrumenta sunt, quibus ipsa agit, propterea quòd forma essentialis est corporis poris

page.notes: Marginal note "Cap.3." in the left margin, beside the line "cet Philosophus" (at the start of the paragraph's third-to-last line region). Its reading is clear. Several words are marked by print irregularities: "stirpis" appears printed as "stirpis"-like form and is read as stirpis; "nô" is printed with a tilde over the o; "quic quam" appears as printed; "poris" is the last word of the page, which continues on the next page. The text reads "conceptus non fit actu animatus" in the scan; the transcription above reads "sit actu" as printed. The line "propterea quod forma essentialis est cor-" is hyphenated at the line end and continues as "poris". Some letters are faint due to ink and paper wear, notably in "uegetalem" and "conceptibus"; they were read as shown but are not fully certain.
